take the tray out with both hands

close the door, turn it off

little.skill: Clean hands and a healthy plate
little.twist: Three vegetables and fruit for the plate this time, and one more question: when do you wash your hands?
little.can_now: wash their hands for 20 seconds, build a healthy plate, cut soft food with a child-safe knife and the bridge grip, and measure a cup

steps.say: The practice kitchen! Today we make {recipe}, from {recipe_from}. In a real kitchen a grown-up is always near. First: clean hands.
Turn on the tap and wet your hands.
Press the soap pump.

steps.label: 20 seconds
steps.say: Rub your hands for 20 seconds: palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs and nails. Hum Happy Birthday twice!
steps.done: 20 seconds! Watch the germs' glow fade away.

steps.say: Rinse the soap off under the water.
Turn the tap off.
Dry your hands on a clean towel.
steps.done: Clean and dry. Ready to cook!

steps.say: The red tap is the hot tap. Its water can be very hot.

choices.text: Cold first, and a grown-up checks it
Turn the hot tap on full
choices.why: Hot water can scald: a grown-up runs the cold first, then checks the water.

steps.done: Cold first, and a grown-up checks the hot tap.

steps.say: When do you wash your hands?

choices.text: Before cooking and eating, and after the toilet

choices.why: Germs are too small to see. Wash before cooking and eating, and after the toilet.

steps.done: Before food, and after the toilet.

steps.say: A healthy plate: half is vegetables and fruit, a quarter is grains like rice or bread, a quarter is protein like beans, eggs or fish. And water to drink.
Fill half the plate with vegetables and fruit. Pick three.
steps.done: Half the plate: vegetables and fruit.

steps.say: Fill half the plate with vegetables and fruit. Pick two.
steps.done: Half the plate: vegetables and fruit.

steps.say: A quarter of the plate: grains. Pick one.
The last quarter: protein. Pick one.
What is the best drink with your meal?

choices.why: Fizzy drinks have lots of sugar. Water is best.

steps.say: How do you hold the food to cut it?

choices.text: The bridge: fingers and thumb make a bridge, the knife goes under it
Fingers in front of the knife
choices.why: Keep fingers out of the knife's way: make a bridge and cut under it.

steps.say: Cut {cut_food} with the child-safe knife, under the bridge: slowly, back and forth.
Pour {pour_words} of {pour_what} into the measuring cup. Stop at the line.
Stir it all together in the bowl.
Now clean up: wipe the table with the cloth.
Your baby cousin Nia is coming to play. Babies put things in their mouths, and small things can get stuck and stop them breathing.

lines.small_wheel: A little toy wheel: into the box.

steps.say: Help a grown-up tidy away the small things on the floor, before Nia comes.
steps.done: All the small things are up high, out of Nia's reach.

lines.small_wheel: A little toy wheel: into the box.
lines.small_battery: A tiny round battery: give it to a grown-up.

steps.say: Find all 5 small things Nia could put in her mouth.
steps.done: All 5, even the tiny battery: well spotted!

steps.say: A snack for Nia: grapes. How does a grown-up give them to a little child?

choices.why: Whole grapes can get stuck in a small child's throat: grown-ups cut them into quarters.

steps.done: Cut small, and Nia sits down to eat.

steps.say: You did it! Clean hands for 20 seconds, a healthy plate, a safe cut and a measured cup. Enjoy your {recipe}!

check.say: How long do you rub your hands with soap?
What fills half a healthy plate?
How do you hold food to cut it?

name_it.title: Clean hands, a healthy plate
lines: Wash with soap for 20 seconds, rinse, dry.
Half the plate vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains, a quarter protein.
Cut with a child-safe knife and the bridge grip, a grown-up near.
Small things up high, away from babies; a grown-up cuts grapes small.
name_it.source: The WHO's healthy diet and hand-washing advice, and the UK's Eatwell Guide

little.try_real: Show your grown-up your 20-second hand wash before the next meal (hum Happy Birthday twice). Then help them put the meal on the plate: half vegetables and fruit!

sources.fact: Small things such as marbles, coins, button batteries and small toy parts can choke a baby or toddler: keep them out of reach; cut grapes and other small round foods lengthways into quarters for young children.
sources.source: Child Accident Prevention Trust, choking; NHS, choking in babies and children

sources.fact: Hot tap water can scald: run the cold first and check the temperature; a grown-up checks water for a child.
sources.source: Child Accident Prevention Trust, burns and scalds

sources.fact: Wash hands with soap and water: wet, apply soap, rub all surfaces (palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs, nails) for at least 20 seconds, rinse, dry with a clean towel.
sources.source: CDC, clean hands: how to wash your hands

sources.fact: Hand washing takes about 20 seconds: about as long as singing Happy Birthday twice.
sources.source: NHS, how to wash your hands

sources.fact: A healthy diet has plenty of fruit and vegetables (at least 400 g a day), whole grains and pulses, and little free sugar and salt.
A healthy plate: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains, a quarter healthy protein, and water to drink.
sources.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, the Healthy Eating Plate

sources.fact: Children learn the bridge hold and the claw grip to cut food safely, with supervision.
sources.source: British Nutrition Foundation, Food - a fact of life (cooking skills)

middle.twist: The scales show 35 with the empty bowl on them: press zero first.
middle.can_now: weigh and measure ingredients, cut with the claw grip, whisk, and use a hob safely with a grown-up: handles in, a low heat, the hot light

steps.say: The practice kitchen. Today: {recipe}, from {recipe_from}. A grown-up is always with you at the hob. Clean hands first.
Wet your hands and press the soap pump.

steps.label: 20 seconds
steps.say: Rub for 20 seconds: palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs and nails.
Rinse and dry on a clean towel.
The scales show 35 with the empty bowl on them. Press zero first.
steps.done: Zero. Now it weighs only the food.

steps.say: Spoon {weigh_what} onto the scales until it reads {weigh_g} grams. Slowly near the end!
Pour {pour_words} of {pour_what}.
To slice {cut_food}, which grip keeps your fingers safe?

choices.why: Flat fingers can slip under the knife. Tuck the fingertips in like a claw.

steps.say: Slice {cut_food}, the claw holding it and the knife going up and down.
Whisk it in the bowl, quickly back and forth.
The pan's handle sticks out over the edge. Turn it in, away from the edge.
steps.done: Handle in: nobody can knock it.

steps.say: With your grown-up, turn the knob to low.

steps.label: cooking
steps.say: It cooks. Stay with the hob: never leave cooking alone.
Done: turn the knob off.
The hob is off, but the hot light is still on. What does it mean?

choices.text: It is still hot: don't touch

choices.why: The hot light means the hob is still hot. Never touch it until the light is off.

steps.done: Still hot. Keep hands away until the light goes off.

steps.say: Practice time: on another day, the oil in a pan catches fire. In real life you get out and tell a grown-up: they do this. Here you practise, so you know why.
First, turn the heat off, if you can reach it safely.

safe_mistake.wrong: throwing water on a pan fire
safe_mistake.why: Water makes burning oil jump up in a big flare of flame. That's why we put a lid on it.
safe_mistake.right: Slide the lid on to cover the pan, and leave it.

steps.say: The flames are still there. What puts them out?
steps.done: The lid keeps the air out: the fire goes out.

safe_mistake.wrong: throwing water on a pan fire
safe_mistake.why: Water makes burning oil jump up in a big flare of flame. That's why we put a lid on it.
safe_mistake.right: Slide the lid on to cover the pan, and leave it.

steps.say: Heat off, and the flames are still there. What now?
steps.done: The lid, all by yourself: the fire is out.

steps.say: The fire is out under the lid. Now?

choices.text: Leave it covered until it is cold

choices.why: Air can make it flare up again: leave the lid on until the pan is cold.

choices.text: Carry the pan to the sink
choices.why: Never move a burning or hot pan: leave it where it is, covered.

steps.say: And if a pan fire doesn't go out, or gets bigger?

choices.why: Never water on a pan fire. Get out, close the door behind you, and call {number}.

steps.say: Clean up: wipe the table.
Well done! You weighed and measured, cut with the claw, whisked, and used the hob safely with a grown-up.

check.say: To weigh flour, the scales first show...
Which grip keeps fingers safe when slicing?
A pan's handle on the hob points...
The hob's hot light is on. You...

name_it.title: Measure, cut, cook safely
lines: Scales at zero, then weigh; cups in fractions.
Cut with the claw grip, slowly.
At the hob: a grown-up there, handles in, low heat, never left alone; the hot light means still hot.
A pan fire: heat off, a lid on, leave it covered. Never water.
name_it.source: The WHO's food safety keys, the British Nutrition Foundation's cooking skills, and home safety advice (RoSPA)

middle.try_real: Cook {recipe} with your grown-up: you weigh and measure, you slice with the claw, and you turn the pan's handle in. Your grown-up does the hob with you.

sources.fact: A small pan fire: turn off the heat if it is safe, slide a lid over the pan and leave it covered until it is completely cool; never throw water on burning oil.
If a pan fire doesn't go out or spreads: get out, close the door, stay out and call 999 or 112.
sources.source: London Fire Brigade, kitchen fire safety

sources.fact: Keep clean: wash your hands before handling food and often during food preparation.
sources.source: WHO, Five Keys to Safer Food

sources.fact: The claw grip and the bridge hold are the safe knife grips taught to children, who cook with an adult supervising.
sources.source: British Nutrition Foundation, Food - a fact of life (cooking skills)

sources.fact: Turn pan handles inwards, away from the edge of the cooker, and use the back rings where you can; never leave cooking unattended.
sources.source: RoSPA (Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents), home safety

sources.fact: Hot drinks, pans and hobs cause most scalds to children at home; a hob stays hot after it is switched off.
sources.source: Child Accident Prevention Trust, burns and scalds

big.skill: Cook a meal and plan a week
big.twist: The kettle is filled above MAX: tip some out. And the week's money is tighter.
big.can_now: keep food safe (raw and cooked apart, the fridge cold), use a kettle and an oven safely, cook a meal and plan a week's meals on a budget

steps.say: The practice kitchen. Today: {recipe}, from {recipe_from}, and a plan for the week. Hands washed? Let's keep food safe.

steps.label: 20 seconds
steps.say: Soap and 20 seconds of rubbing, then rinse.
steps.done: Clean hands. Wash again after touching raw meat or eggs.

steps.say: You cut raw chicken and salad. How many chopping boards?

choices.text: Two: raw meat on its own board

choices.why: Germs from raw meat can get onto food you eat raw. Keep raw meat on its own board, or wash it well between.

steps.say: Raw meat goes on the bottom shelf of the fridge, so it can't drip onto other food. Put it there.
How cold should a fridge be?

choices.why: Germs grow fast when it is warm. A fridge keeps food at 5 °C or below.

steps.say: Fill the kettle at the tap, between MIN and MAX.
Someone filled this kettle above MAX. What do you do?

choices.text: Tip some out to below MAX

choices.why: Above MAX, boiling water can spit out. Tip some out first.

steps.say: Close the lid and switch it on. Keep the cord away from the edge.

steps.label: boiling
steps.say: It boils, then switches itself off. Stand back from the steam.
Pour {pour_words} of hot water into the pan, slowly and away from you.
steps.done: Slowly and steadily. Kettle back on its base.

steps.say: Weigh {weigh_g} grams of {weigh_what}.
Slice {cut_food} with the claw grip.
The roasted vegetables are ready. Oven gloves on first.
Open the oven door and step back from the hot air.
steps.done: Open. Hot air comes out: wait a moment.

steps.say: Take the tray out with both gloved hands.
Put it on the heat mat.
Close the door and turn the oven off.
Practice time: a splash of hot water lands on Bobo's paw. Burns and scalds need cooling, straight away.
Hold Bobo's paw under cool running water.

steps.label: 20 minutes
steps.say: Cool running water for 20 minutes: that's how long a burn needs. Let's speed up the clock.
steps.done: Twenty minutes of cool running water.

steps.say: Then?

choices.text: Cover it loosely with cling film, and tell a grown-up

choices.why: Never butter, ice or creams: cool running water for 20 minutes, then cling film.

steps.done: Loosely covered, and a grown-up decides if it needs a doctor.

steps.say: Now plan a week of meals with pretend coins. Needs first: the food for the meals. Then a treat only if there is money left.
Money is tighter this week: 19 coins. Put the needs in the basket: rice, lentils, vegetables, eggs and milk. Then PAY.
steps.done: Needs first, and it fits: 18 of 19 coins.

steps.say: You have 23 coins. Put the week's needs in the basket: rice, lentils, vegetables, eggs and milk. One treat fits too. Then PAY.
steps.done: The week's food, within the budget!

steps.say: Rice: one 2 kg bag for 6 coins, or two 1 kg bags for 4 coins each. Which is the better buy?

choices.text: The 2 kg bag: 3 coins a kilo

choices.why: Two small bags cost 8 coins for 2 kg: 4 a kilo. The big bag is 3 a kilo.

steps.done: Compare the price per kilo. The big bag saves 2 coins.

steps.say: Brilliant! Food kept safe, the kettle and the oven used safely, a meal cooked, and a week's shopping on a budget. Pretend coins today; real money with your grown-up.

check.say: Raw chicken and salad: chopping boards?
To take a hot tray out of the oven, you use...

name_it.title: Cook safely, plan wisely
lines: Keep clean: wash hands, and again after raw meat or eggs.
Separate raw and cooked: raw meat on its own board, at the bottom of the fridge.
Keep food cold: the fridge at 5 °C or below.
Kettle between MIN and MAX; oven gloves; a grown-up there.
Plan the week: needs first, compare the price per kilo.
name_it.source: The WHO's Five Keys to Safer Food, the UK Food Standards Agency, and money basics (the OECD/INFE framework)

big.try_real: With your grown-up, plan three dinners for next week, write the shopping list (needs first) and check the prices per kilo in the shop. Then cook one of them together.

sources.fact: Burns and scalds: cool under cool running water for 20 minutes, remove anything near it that isn't stuck, cover loosely with cling film; never ice, butter or creams.
The Five Keys to Safer Food: keep clean; separate raw and cooked; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water and raw materials.
sources.source: WHO, Five Keys to Safer Food manual

sources.fact: Keep the fridge at 5 °C or below; store raw meat and poultry covered on the bottom shelf so it can't drip onto other food.
Never fill a kettle above its MAX mark; keep the cord away from the worktop's edge; hot drinks and kettles cause many scalds to children.
sources.source: Child Accident Prevention Trust, burns and scalds

sources.fact: Planning and managing money: a budget, needs before wants, comparing prices (such as the unit price).
sources.source: OECD/INFE Core Competencies Framework on Financial Literacy for Youth (2015)
